question_text: One week after delivery, a 3550-g (7-lb 13-oz) newborn has multiple episodes of bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. He passed urine 14 hours after delivery and had his first bowel movement 3 days after delivery. He was born at term to a 31-year-old woman. Pregnancy was uncomplicated and the mother received adequate prenatal care. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 132/min, and respirations are 50/min. Examination shows a distended abdomen. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Digital rectal examination shows a patent anus and an empty rectum. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following is the underlying cause of these findings?

                    ### Question
                    One week after delivery, a 3550-g (7-lb 13-oz) newborn has multiple episodes of bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. He passed urine 14 hours after delivery and had his first bowel movement 3 days after delivery. He was born at term to a 31-year-old woman. Pregnancy was uncomplicated and the mother received adequate prenatal care. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 132/min, and respirations are 50/min. Examination shows a distended abdomen. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Digital rectal examination shows a patent anus and an empty rectum. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following is the underlying cause of these findings?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Defective migration of neural crest cells
opb. Disruption of blood flow to the fetal jejunum
opc. Mutation in the CFTR gene
opd. Abnormal rotation of the intestine
ope. Failed recanalization of the fetal duodenum

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The newborn's symptoms of bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and delayed passage of meconium suggest a significant intestinal obstruction. The presence of an empty rectum indicates that the obstruction is likely proximal to the rectum. The most common cause of such obstruction in a newborn, particularly with these symptoms, is failed recanalization of the fetal duodenum, which can lead to duodenal atresia. This aligns with the consensus that obstruction due to failed recanalization is a well-documented condition in neonates presenting with these clinical signs. Other options, such as defective migration of neural crest cells or abnormal rotation of the intestine, do not directly correlate with the specific presentation of bilious vomiting and delayed meconium passage in this case.
